title: ATMOS 2008 Abstracts Collection - 8th Workshop on Algorithmic Approaches for Transportation Modeling, Optimization, and Systems
contribution: Editorial: the ATMOS 2008 abstracts collection edited by Fischetti and Widmayer, whose own text is a one-line abstract and the preface paragraph; the twelve collected abstracts (railway robustness, delay management, timetable information, line planning, rolling stock, airport gate and bus assignment, periodic and Lagrangian timetabling) are by other authors.
problem_entry: n/a (editorial); the editors frame ATMOS as an established series of meetings between algorithms researchers working on transportation and practitioners, mainly from railways (p. 1).
key_idea: n/a (editorial compilation: one-line abstract, the preface as an item, then each paper's abstract, keywords, author line and link, pp. 1-7).
positioning: n/a for the editors; the collected abstracts (other authors' voices) include a Benders lower bound on the price of recoverability for NS rolling stock by Cacchiani, Caprara, Galli, Kroon and Maróti (p. 5), and Chvátal closures of the PESP (p. 7).
writing: Editorial format; the only text in the editors' voice is the one-line abstract and the preface paragraph (p. 1).

quotes.text: The series of ATMOS workshops, starting in Heraklion in 2001, continuing in Malaga in 2002, Budapest in 2003, Bergen in 2004, Palma de Mallorca in 2005, Zürich in 2006, and Sevilla in 2007 is by now an established series of meetings between algorithms researchers dealing with transportation problems, and practitioners, mainly from railways.

title: Projected Chvátal–Gomory cuts for mixed integer linear programs
contribution: Introduces projected Chvátal-Gomory cuts (CG cuts of the LP relaxation projected onto the integer variables), proves that their closure equals the split cuts with one empty disjunction side and that combinatorial Benders cuts are among them, and measures by MIP-based separation that the closure closes about 29% of the gap on mixed MIPLIB 3.0 instances (more than 70% on TW-ATSP) and adds to GMI, MIR and lift-and-project cuts.
problem_entry: Fischetti and Lodi's MIP-based CG separation shows the first Chvátal closure of an ILP is often tight, but the model does not extend to the GMI closure of a MILP, whose separation is nonlinear or parametric; does the tightness carry over to MILP? (abstract p. 1; pp. 2-3)
key_idea: Project the LP relaxation onto the integer variables and take CG cuts of the projection (multipliers u >= 0 with u^T C >= 0): the separation MILP is the Fischetti-Lodi model plus one constraint family, accepting a family theoretically dominated by GMI cuts (abstract p. 1; pp. 3-4).
assumptions: MILP (7) with integer x >= 0 and continuous y >= 0, rational data (p. 4); best fit when the continuous variables only express feasibility, often through big-M, and are absent from the objective, e.g. TW-ATSP and map labeling (pp. 3, 6-7); 43 mixed-integer MIPLIB 3.0 instances and 21 Ascheuer stacker-crane TW-ATSP instances on a weak degree-only model (pp. 9, 12, 14).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: pro-CG closure = P intersected with all split cuts having one empty disjunction side, by two inclusions through the CG procedure, pp. 5-6

Finite-rank argument: with continuous variables absent from the objective, every valid inequality in x has finite Chvátal rank w.r.t. the projection, so iterated pro-CG cuts alone solve the MILP, p. 6
Theorem 2: combinatorial Benders cuts are pro-CG cuts (the maximum of sum x_i over P stays below |Q|), p. 8
Two-variable polytope showing when pro-CG cuts help (max x) and when they cannot (max y), p. 6
Rank-1 membership check by maximizing a known inequality's left-hand side over the LP (infeasible-path 3.95, tournament 3.9875, both rounded to 3), pp. 8-9
Pure cutting-plane loop with separation MILP solved by CPLEX 9.0 (mip emphasis 4), aborted when the incumbent stalls, p. 9
experiments: 3.2 GHz Pentium 4, 1,200 s per run, % gap closed: on MIPLIB 3.0 closure reached on 10, limit hit on 26, no pro-CG cut on 7; about 29% over 41 instances (none on 11, about 40% on the other 30); against one round of COIN-OR GMI (24%) and MIR (23%) cuts and Bonami-Minoux lift-and-project (35%), adding pro-CG cuts gives 41%, 40%, 49%, and all combined 55% instead of 48%; TW-ATSP more than 70% on every instance, limit reached on all, share of time to the final bound reported (pp. 9, 11, 14).
positioning: Extends Fischetti-Lodi [16] from ILP to MILP; places pro-CG cuts against the GMI/split closure (Cook-Kannan-Schrijver [11], Nemhauser-Wolsey [24], Cornuéjols-Li [12, 13]) and the nonlinear [14] or parametric [4] GMI separation; subsumes Codato-Fischetti CB cuts [9] and Ascheuer-Fischetti-Grötschel tournament inequalities [2] (pp. 2-3, 5, 8-9).
writing: Theory first, then computation; the expected fit is offered as a conjecture ('it can be conjectured', p. 3); small examples carry the intuition (pp. 6, 8-9); the conclusion opens its findings by conceding ineffective cases (p. 15).
limits_future: No pro-CG cut exists on 7 instances and none helps on 11; proving that none remains can need much enumeration; future: faster heuristic separation, use beside special-purpose separators, scheduling and cutting/packing models with big-M links (pp. 9, 11-12, 14-15).

method_links.note: Practice, joint: which cut to add is a MILP solved heuristically (aborted on stalling, mip emphasis 4) by the same general-purpose solver (step 2), to measure a closure's potential before asking for efficient separation (step 4); the time limit is hit on 26 of 43 MIPLIB instances and on every TW-ATSP instance, the cost listed under the method's limitations.

Joint: the continuous variables of big-M models are diagnosed as expressing feasibility only and projected out (steps 1 and 3), but the projection yields a cut family in the x space rather than a thinner model; Theorem 2 ties it to Codato-Fischetti's Benders-type cuts.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A cut family theoretically dominated by GMI cuts is chosen because its separation stays a MILP of the Fischetti-Lodi form that already worked, with one extra constraint family.

transferable: To carry a MIP-based separation from pure to mixed-integer programs, require u^T C >= 0 on the multipliers: this projects out the continuous variables and adds one constraint family to the separation model (p. 4).
Locate a new cut family exactly, by a closure-equality theorem (split cuts with one empty side, p. 5) and by showing that a known family is a special case (CB cuts, p. 8).
Test whether a known inequality is a rank-1 member of the family by maximizing its left-hand side over the LP and checking that the maximum rounds down to the right-hand side (pp. 8-9).
Report a new cut family alone, added to each standard family, and added to all of them; the increments show whether it is genuinely different (pp. 11-12).
When runs hit the time limit, report the share of the limit spent before the final bound was found (p. 14).
coauthors: Pierre Bonami, Gérard Cornuéjols, Sanjeeb Dash, Andrea Lodi

quotes.text: Though theoretically dominated by GMI cuts, projected CG cuts have the advantage of producing a separation model very similar to the one introduced by Fischetti and Lodi, whose solution can typically be carried out in a reasonable amount of computing time.
This indicates that the pro-CG cuts are genuinely different from those that are currently used in MILP solvers and that it is worth exploring heuristics that generate them more efficiently.

title: Repairing MIP infeasibility through local branching
contribution: A feasibility-pump-plus-local-branching hybrid that warm-starts local branching from the pump's infeasible point through a Phase-I relaxation with one violation-scaled binary artificial per violated row; on 44 MIPLIB 2003 and 39 further 0-1 MIPs it finds a first feasible solution faster than CPLEX 9.0.3 in 44 cases and slower in 21, and it yields a small set of constraints whose removal makes an infeasible MIP feasible.
problem_entry: LB and RINS need a starting feasible solution, an issue for difficult MIPs; the pump gives an almost-feasible point cheaply, and where it stalls one can switch to enumeration; secondly, the repair is a MIP analogue of maximum-feasible-subsystem analysis for LP (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Phase I transplanted: relax each row violated by the start to a_i^T x + delta_i y_i >= b_i (delta_i its violation, y_i binary), minimize sum y_i, and let LB, whose constraint acts on all binaries including the y's, drive the count to zero; big-M artificials and a weighted cost-plus-infeasibility objective were tried and set aside (pp. 1-2, 4).
assumptions: 0-1 MIP with a nonempty binary set (needed by LB), general integers and continuous variables allowed (p. 1); 44 0-1 MIPLIB 2003 instances plus 39 hard 0-1 MIPs, some received by personal communication; stp3d and 11 instances solved by every algorithm in 0.0 s excluded with reasons (pp. 5, 9-10).
proof_devices: Phase-I relaxation a_i^T x + delta_i y_i >= b_i with delta_i the violation at the start point, objective sum y_i; the start is feasible with value |T|, p. 4
Asymmetric local branching constraint (11), counting only 1->0 flips, for small-support covering-like relaxations, pp. 4-5
Adaptive neighbourhood size k = floor(|T'|/2), k = 10 below 20 violated rows; 30 s per neighbourhood, p. 5
Start quality controlled by truncating FP at 0, 10 or 100 iterations (LB0, LB10, LB100), p. 5
experiments: CPLEX 9.0.3 and FP as baselines, Pentium M 1.6 GHz notebook, 1,800 s, stop at the first feasible solution; LB100 at least as fast as the other variants in 58 cases (47, 40); LB100 strictly faster than CPLEX in 44 cases, slower in 21; failures 4 (CPLEX) vs 3 (LB100); CPLEX's first solution typically better in quality, not tabulated; single runs, sub-second differences counted (pp. 5-8).
positioning: Extends the authors' own LB [9] with FP [10] (Fischetti-Glover-Lodi); RINS [7] named as another refining heuristic that needs an incumbent; model repair placed next to max-feasible-subsystem and IIS work for LP [2, 6, 12]; LB confirmations by Hansen-Mladenović-Urošević and Fischetti-Polo-Scantamburlo (pp. 2-3).
writing: The Phase I analogy frames the method in the abstract and introduction (pp. 1-2); design choices justified by a tested alternative (big-M) and a preliminary study (weighted objective) (p. 4); no conclusions section in this version (pp. 6-9).
limits_future: The original objective is disregarded, so the feasible solution 'can be arbitrarily bad'; binaries required; no future-work statement (pp. 1, 4, 6-9).

method_links.note: Practice, joint: the repair is itself a MIP (the model plus one binary artificial per violated row), explored inside LB neighbourhoods by the black-box solver (step 2); thin code on the CPLEX callable libraries (step 3).

Practice, joint: 'we avoided any parameter tuning', FP exactly as published (step 5); exclusions by a rule every algorithm shares, listed by name (step 3); losses printed: CPLEX faster on 21 instances and better in first-solution quality (step 6). Whether CPLEX ran with a heuristic emphasis is not stated (step 2).

Dated lapse (2004-05, joint): single runs per instance and win counts that include sub-second differences (harp2: 0.0 s for CPLEX against 0.8 s), read without any measure of spread; predates the 2012 statement.
The feasibility requirement is moved from the constraints into the objective, as in Phase I.

The skill's pump anatomy dates the return of enumeration in place of random flips to 2007; this preprint, dated February 16, 2004, already switches from the pump's almost-feasible point to enumeration by LB.
The same text calls LB 'a heuristic approach' and its strategy 'exact in nature': the heuristic reading is partly the authors' own framing.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Phase-I relaxation with violation-scaled binary artificials
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An infeasible start is made feasible in a relaxed model whose artificials are binaries scaled by each row's violation, so a binary neighbourhood search can count and remove violations; avoids choosing a big-M weight.

transferable: To warm-start a binary neighbourhood search from an infeasible point, add one binary per violated row scaled by that row's violation at the point, minimize their sum, and let the search treat them like any other binaries; no big-M weight has to be chosen (p. 4).
Tie the neighbourhood size to the current violation count (k = floor(|T'|/2), with a floor of 10 below 20 violations) so that the first steps from a badly infeasible start are not slow (p. 5).
Measure a method's sensitivity to the quality of its start by truncating the upstream heuristic at fixed iteration counts (0, 10, 100) and running the method from each (p. 5).
Fix the exclusions of a first-solution study by a rule every arm shares (every algorithm at 0.0 s) and list them by name (p. 5).

quotes.text: The basic idea of the method presented in this section is that the LB algorithm does not necessarily need to start with a feasible solution—a partially feasible one can be a valid warm start for the method.

In our experiments, we avoided any parameter tuning–FP was implemented exactly as in [10], and for the modified LB code we used a time limit of 30 CPU seconds for the exploration of each local-branching neighborhood.

title: The linear ordering problem with cumulative costs
contribution: Defines the linear ordering problem with cumulative costs from a UMTS power-control and detection-order application, proves it NP-hard, and solves all application instances exactly with a plain backward permutation enumeration that beats a big-M MIP solved by CPLEX 9.0.2 by up to three orders of magnitude, CPLEX also returning wrong answers on some instances despite tightened tolerances.
problem_entry: An application (joint SIC detection order and power control in UMTS) fits neither HP nor LOP; a GRASP heuristic existed, and benchmarking it was the initial motivation (pp. 2, 4-6, 18).
key_idea: Model the backward cumulative propagation exactly (LOP-CC, BLOP-CC with a power bound) and solve it two ways: a GRL-based MIP linearizing y_ij = alpha_j x_ij with big-M = U, and a depth-first enumeration from the last position whose parametric bound adds alpha times the costs of the unplaced nodes, warm-started by a FIFO queue (pp. 3, 6, 11-14).
assumptions: Complete digraph, nonnegative node weights and arc costs; BLOP-CC may be infeasible (p. 3); 4 scenarios x 500 random interference matrices for 16 users in a 580 m cell (log-distance path loss), 8 sizes n = 2..16 each; 16 users is the realistic maximum; matrices published (pp. 14, 16).
proof_devices: Reduction from directed Hamiltonian path with p_i = 1 and c_ij in {M, 2M}; induction bound pi(P_n) <= M^{n-1} + 4^n M^{n-2} for good paths against 2M^{n-1}; M = 4^n + 1 keeps the size polynomial, pp. 9-10
Corollary for BLOP-CC with U = UB_good, p. 11
Linearization y_ij = alpha_j x_ij with M = U; the redundant y_ij <= U x_ij kept for numerical stability, pp. 11-12
Parametric lower bound (20) for partial permutations built backwards, pp. 13-14
Tightened CPLEX tolerances (absolute gap 1e-13, relative gap 1e-11, integrality, optimality, feasibility 1e-9), p. 16
experiments: Enumeration vs CPLEX 9.0.2 on the MIP, Pentium M 1.4 GHz notebook; per set and size: instances solved, average and maximum time, speedup and '# fails' (instances CPLEX did not solve correctly, up to 37 of 2,000 at n = 12); up to three orders of magnitude faster, CPLEX never faster; the MIP arm ran on 50 and on 2-5 instances per set at n = 14 and 16, selection not stated; enumeration solves n = 20 in about 4 hours (pp. 16-17).
positioning: Generalizes HP and LOP; the MIP is derived from the Grötschel-Jünger-Reinelt LOP model [3]; the application and the GRASP to be benchmarked come from Benvenuto-Carnevale-Tomasin [1] (pp. 2, 4-5, 11, 18).
writing: 'for the first time' in abstract and introduction (pp. 1-2); an outline of the proof before the formal one (p. 9); implementation choices justified in one sentence each (pp. 12-13); the numerics problem stated frankly ('we could not fix this pathological situation', p. 16).
limits_future: All application instances solved; the GRASP benchmarked as a byproduct but no GRASP figures given; future: a stronger MIP formulation, sharper pruning, more complex nonlinear costs on the LOP (pp. 16-18).

method_links.note: Practice, joint: the general-purpose solver is asked first, on a MIP with tightened tolerances, and its failures are printed; here the black box loses on numerics and time and the answer is an ad hoc exact enumeration, the step-5 outcome reported as counts of wrong answers rather than stated as a lesson.

Practice, joint: fitting the instances (at most 16 users) leads to no model at all: a plain enumeration chosen 'rather than more sophisticated ones' because its bound is cheap; the step-2 choice is made between algorithms, not formulations.
Dated lapse (2004, joint): at the two largest sizes the MIP arm is timed on a subsample (50 and 2-5 instances per set against 500) without a stated rule.
The exact enumeration doubles as the independent check that counts the MIP solver's wrong answers.
A partner's application first (Padova telecom group), and a new problem class defined from it.
Numerics and exactness are listed as his blind spot; here (2004, joint) default CPLEX tolerances are found too loose, tightened, and the remaining wrong answers counted.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Count the solver's wrong answers against an exact check
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 1 carries a '# fails' column for instances CPLEX did not solve correctly despite tightened tolerances, counted against the exact enumeration (up to 37 of 2,000 at n = 12).

transferable: When a recursive cost forces big-M products into a linear model, check whether building solutions in the order of the recursion (here backwards from the last position) gives each partial solution an exact, cheap bound increment; a plain depth-first search with that bound can beat the MIP by orders of magnitude (pp. 13-14, 16).
Warm-start a permutation enumeration by holding the candidate set in a FIFO queue initialised with a heuristic permutation (p. 14).

When coefficients span orders of magnitude, set the MIP solver's tolerances explicitly, keep redundant linking rows if they stabilize it, and report the number of instances it solved incorrectly against an exact independent method (pp. 12, 16-17).
Publish the generator's raw input (here the interference matrices) so that every derived instance can be rebuilt (p. 16).

quotes.text: We chose this method to enumerate permutations, rather than more sophisticated ones, because we can compute very quickly a parametric lower bound for partial permutations (to be used for pruning purposes), thus enumerating very effectively a large number of nodes.
Since the default ILOG-Cplex tolerances are too large to solve correctly even small instances, we used the following parameter setting (all other parameters being left at default values):

title: How tight is the corner relaxation?
contribution: The first computation of the optimal values of Gomory's corner relaxation (in a vertex-based form immune to degeneracy) and of the group relaxation on MIPLIB 3.0/2003 and Atamtürk's knapsack instances, with a strong NP-hardness proof: the corner bound closes 34.48% of the gap on average against 23.61% for the group bound, is tight mainly for general-integer models and weak for 0-1 ones.
problem_entry: Forty years of theory on the group and corner relaxations, but their practical tightness had never been computed (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Define the corner relaxation by dropping the constraints not binding at an optimal LP vertex (basis-independent, so degeneracy cannot weaken it) and compute it and the group relaxation by brute force with a commercial branch-and-cut code (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: MILP min{c^T x : Ax <= b, x_j integer, j in J}, rational data (p. 1); testbed of Fischetti-Saturni [6]: MIPLIB 3.0 and 2003 minus instances with unknown optimum, negative lower bounds or LP files over 1.7 MB, plus Atamtürk's bounded and unbounded multiple-knapsack instances (p. 3).
proof_devices: Proposition 1, strong NP-hardness, by reduction from Decoding of Linear Codes: d = 1 WLOG, binaries replaced by y >= 0 integer, an MILP whose LP has the unique nondegenerate vertex (1/2, 0), so the corner relaxation is the mod-2 problem; covers the group relaxation too, pp. 2-3
Vertex-based definition (drop the nonbinding rows) immune to primal degeneracy, pp. 1-2
Bias-removing control column GMI′ (one round of GMI cuts on the group-relaxation system), p. 4
Bound checkpoints at 1, 3, 5, 10 hours (one day for group) to argue that time-limited bounds are near-final, pp. 4, 8
experiments: CPLEX 9.1 default, presolve off, AMD Athlon 4200+, 10 h limit (1 h for Atamtürk): % gap closed by one round of GMI cuts, k-cuts (k = 1-50) and k = 60 cuts (both from [6]), GMI′, corner and group; corner 34.48% vs group 23.61% average, GMI′ 9.67% vs GMI 25.32%; pure 0-1 models gain little; z and memory-fault entries marked; my recomputation from the extracted rows reproduces the corner and group averages (34.47%, 23.50%) but not GMI and GMI′ (about 28.8%, 11.3%), and Table 5 repeats Table 4's GMI and GMI′ averages (59.87, 58.66) though its rows average 56.24 and 55.04 (pp. 3-10).
positioning: Fills a gap in the Gomory-Johnson line [8-12, 15]: theory well studied, practice unexplored; credits the complexity result as implicit in earlier work (Letchford [16]) and Balas [3] for the 0-1 weakness; uses the Fischetti-Saturni testbed and cut columns [6] (pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: A short note: the question as title, 'for the first time' in the abstract, one proposition with a half-page proof, five tables and a three-paragraph summary; the referee's suggested comparison is credited (pp. 1-5).
limits_future: Relaxations 1-2 orders of magnitude slower to solve than the original problems, so dynamic programming or basis reduction should be applied; the enumerative approach cannot optimize over the intersection with the LP polyhedron, which needs a dual approach (pp. 3-4).

method_links.note: Practice, joint: the potential of a relaxation is measured with a stock solver at default settings before anyone builds separation for it, and offered as a go or no-go for the research line ('to study (or not to study)') (step 4).
Joint: the bias of the comparison in favour of the GMI cuts is printed and removed by the referee-suggested GMI′ arm, which splits the effect into two readable differences (step 6).

The corner relaxation thins by dropping every nonbinding row; for 0-1 models this drops too much, and nonbinding constraints 'become quite relevant even after just one round of GMI cuts': a limit on deleting constraints from a relaxation, not on deleting variables from a model.
Weak: the abstract and the summary end on where the bound is tight (general integers) and where it is not (many binaries).

transferable: Before building a separator for a relaxation, compute the relaxation's optimum by brute force on a standard testbed and report the gap closed next to the standard cut families (pp. 3-4).
When a time limit stops a bound computation, print the bound at several checkpoints (1, 3, 5, 10 hours) to show that it has flattened (p. 4; Table 3, p. 8).
When a comparison is structurally biased toward one arm, add a control arm that removes the bias (here GMI cuts applied to the relaxed system) and read the two differences separately (p. 4).
Define a basis-dependent relaxation from the LP vertex instead (drop the nonbinding rows), so that primal degeneracy cannot weaken it (pp. 1-2).

quotes.text: Nevertheless, we believe that knowing the quality of the bound that can be achieved on a large set of test cases is important to give the researchers further motivations to study (or not to study) the corner and group relaxations.
This comparison is however biased in favor of the GMI cuts, since they are used in conjunction with the other inequalities of the LP relaxation.

title: ATMOS 2008 Preface--8th Workshop on Algorithmic Approaches for Transportation Modeling, Optimization, and Systems
contribution: Editorial preface to the ATMOS 2008 proceedings (OASIcs vol. 9), co-signed with Widmayer: workshop history and scope, 12 of 15 submissions accepted by the program committee he co-chaired, and an invited talk on timetabling and robustness.
problem_entry: n/a (editorial); scope: complex, large-scale network optimization problems in transportation, mainly railways, needing ideas from mathematical optimization and theoretical computer science (p. 4).
positioning: n/a; frames ATMOS around graph and network algorithms, combinatorial optimization, approximation and online algorithms, stochastic and robust optimization, and the integration of planning stages (pp. 4-5).
writing: Standard preface: history, a scope list of fourteen topics, submission statistics, committee, invited talk, thanks (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: The focus of ATMOS is on complex and large-scale network optimization problems that require new solution techniques and ideas from mathematical optimization and theoretical computer science.
We received 15 submissions, out of which 12 were selected for presentation and inclusion in this volume, in a thorough reviewing process guided by the program committee consisting of

title: Robustness in Train Timetabling
contribution: A CTW 2009 extended abstract proposing a Lagrangian heuristic for robust train timetabling on a corridor (buffer arcs rewarded in the objective, clique capacity constraints relaxed) that, scored by the external delay validator of Fischetti-Salvagnin-Zanette, is reported to give smaller cumulative delays at comparable efficiency than that method (smaller in 4 of the 6 reported pairs, my count).
problem_entry: The nominal TTP ignores operational delays that can affect feasibility and quality; plan buffer times that absorb short delays without being too conservative (p. 2).
key_idea: Keep the nominal space-time-graph ILP, add buffer arcs with their own profit to the objective (one weighted efficiency-robustness objective), relax the clique constraints in a Lagrangian way and solve by subgradient optimization, one max-profit path per train (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: One-way corridor; departure/arrival headways, no overtaking; shift and stretch allowed; profit decreasing linearly, train cancelled at nonpositive profit; discretized time; Modane-Milan instances with 100 and 200 trains (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: Lagrangian relaxation of the clique constraints (1.4) with subgradient optimization; Lagrangian profits p_a - sum lambda_C + b_a; per-train max-profit path subproblem, p. 3
experiments: Modane-Milan corridor, 100 and 200 trains; 1000 Lagrangian iterations (< 2000 s) vs Fischetti-Salvagnin-Zanette [3] (2 h limit, precedences unfixed), both scored by [3]'s external delay-scenario validator; three selected solutions per instance with efficiency and cumulative delay; nominal best efficiencies 9297 and 18542 for reference; smaller delay in 4 of 6 rows (my count), the other two rows with higher efficiency (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Builds on the Caprara-Fischetti-Toth Lagrangian TTP heuristic [1]; compares with and borrows the validation method of Fischetti-Salvagnin-Zanette [3]; cites Fischetti-Monaci light robustness [2] (pp. 3-4).
writing: Four-page extended abstract: problem, model, Lagrangian, one table, a one-line outlook; the claim sentence is hedged ('comparable efficiency', 'slightly shorter computing times') (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Preliminary: ongoing tests on other instances and parameter settings; delay not monotone in efficiency; the selection of the three reported solutions not stated (pp. 3-4).

method_links.note: Joint: both arms' solutions pass through the same external validator (the shared-machinery half of step 1), but only three selected solutions per instance are shown with no stated rule, rows pair unequal efficiencies, and the budgets differ (under 2000 s against 2 hours).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: External validator for a surrogate objective
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The buffer-profit objective is a surrogate; robustness is judged by a separate delay-scenario simulation (all trains kept, precedences fixed, cumulative delay) applied to every compared solution.

transferable: Model robustness as extra arcs with their own reward in a path-based timetabling model, so that the Lagrangian subproblem stays one longest-path problem per train (pp. 2-3).
Judge a robustness surrogate by an independent delay-scenario validator applied to all compared solutions, never by the surrogate's own value (p. 3).
Report the nominal optimum next to the robust solutions, so that the efficiency price of robustness can be read off (p. 3).

quotes.text: Roughly speaking, we define a solution to be robust if it allows to avoid delay propagation as much as possible.
As it can be observed, the Lagrangian-based approach finds solutions of comparable efficiency producing smaller cumulative delays than in [3] (in slightly shorter computing times).

title: Mixed-integer programming models for nesting problems
contribution: Shows that the Daniels-Li-Milenkovic MIP for nesting, even with lifted big-M coefficients and clique-building branching priorities, solves only instances with fewer than 10 pieces, and turns this negative result into an approximate MIP for the multiple containment subproblem that, after an LP repair, raises the efficiency of a greedy layout by 0.16 to 2.43 points on garment instances.
problem_entry: Evaluate the viability of modern MIP techniques for practically relevant nesting (sub-)problems; nesting is strongly NP-hard and geometrically hard (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: First the full no-fit-polygon slice MIP with big-M disjunctions, strengthened by coefficient lifting and branching priorities; after it fails, an approximate MIP for placing trims into holes (bounding boxes, usable holes, a cell grid), repaired by a compaction/separation LP with fixed slice choices and solved class by class (pp. 5-23).
assumptions: Simple hole-less polygons, translation only, fixed-height strip of virtually infinite length, length plus an epsilon compaction term; broken-glass instances with known optimum and garment instances available on request (pp. 2-4, 7, 12-13, 25).
proof_devices: Slice partition of each no-fit polygon's complement, one binary per slice, big-M disjunctions; once slices are fixed the problem is an LP, pp. 5-8
Big-M lifting: each coefficient is the facet's maximum over another slice within a bounding box, found at that slice's vertices, pp. 8-10
Clique-building branching priorities passed to the solver's priority mechanism, pp. 11-12
Repair of an approximate placement by fixing the disjunction choices and solving the compaction/separation LP, removing the most overlapping trim if it fails, pp. 22-23
experiments: Broken glass (5, 7, 9 pieces; CPLEX 7.0, AMD Athlon 1.2 GHz, 100,000-node cap), priorities on/off with lifting always on: priorities solve the 7-piece instance, the 9-piece one stays near 59% gap; lifting's limited impact stated without a table; containment MIP-place vs the authors' greedy on three garment instances (four rows): efficiency +2.43, +0.46, +0.55, +0.16 points against the text's 1-2%; run times not tabulated (pp. 13-14, 25, 28).
positioning: Builds on the Daniels-Li-Milenkovic MIP [12, 23] and Li-Milenkovic compaction/separation [24]; places the nesting disjunctions beside scheduling [32] and rectangular packing [31] models; survey by Dowsland and Dowsland [15] (pp. 2, 5, 8, 22).
writing: The negative result is stated plainly ('quite discouraging', p. 13) and becomes the motivation for Section 4 (pp. 2, 14); figures carry the comparison with greedy (pp. 24-30); the conclusion states the lesson in one sentence (pp. 28, 31).
limits_future: MIP not appropriate for real-world nesting, useful for simplified subproblems in heuristics; the simplified model ignores interactions across rows and columns, hence overlaps; future: the line deserves more attention (pp. 21-23, 28, 31).

method_links.note: Practice, joint: when the full MIP cannot meet the requirement, the lesson is printed ('unlikely to be useful' at practical size, step 5) and the MIP moves to one sub-decision of a heuristic, the containment of trims in holes, solved in seconds by the same solver (step 2).

Practice, joint: the simplified containment model is the weaker model that wins for a heuristic (step 2), checked by an exact LP repair (step 6); but the order is reversed: the full model was strengthened first (lifting, priorities) and thinned only after that failed.

Dated lapse (2006-07, joint): the only baseline is the authors' own greedy, on three instances, run times not tabulated, and the per-row gains (2.43, 0.46, 0.55, 0.16 points) do not match the text's 'by 1-2%': one above that range, three below it.
The negative result is stated as a lesson and drives the second half of the paper.
The inferred thesis-to-paper pattern: a 2003 doctoral dissertation (hosted on Fischetti's thesis pages; supervision not stated) became a co-authored journal paper.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Approximate MIP plus exact LP repair
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A geometrically simplified MIP is solved, its combinatorial choices are fixed in the exact model, which leaves an LP (compaction/separation), and the worst-overlapping item is dropped if that LP fails.

transferable: In a disjunctive geometric MIP, lift each big-M coefficient separately: the coefficient of another slice's binary is the facet's maximum over that slice within a bounding box, found at the slice's vertices (pp. 9-10).
Steer a black-box solver without writing a branching rule: give priorities that settle all pairwise relations inside a growing clique of objects before a new object is touched (pp. 11-12).
Build test instances by cutting a known shape into pieces, so that the optimum is known in advance and any remaining gap is the method's (pp. 12-13).

When a full model fails, write an approximate MIP for the subproblem a heuristic solves greedily, then restore exact feasibility by fixing its combinatorial choices in the exact model and solving the remaining LP; remove the worst-overlapping item and repeat if that LP is infeasible (pp. 14, 22-23).
Solve the approximate model per class of similar-sized items, in order of size, where the approximation is accurate (p. 23).

quotes.text: Our main goal is to evaluate the viability of using modern MIP techniques to address practically-relevant nesting (sub-)problems.
It appears clear, however, that the MIP approach (as described) is unlikely to be useful for solving to proven optimality nesting instances of practical size.
